opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the premise. I'm not sure *intricate* orchestration, in the sense of hand-designed pipelines where a human decides this agent plans, that one critiques, and a third retrieves, will stay valuable in the same form. A lot of that scaffolding exists to compensate for things the model can't yet do well, like long-horizon planning, keeping its own state straight, or noticing it went wrong. As the base model gets stronger, many of those crutches turn into overhead. We've already seen that: elaborate prompting tricks that mattered a lot two years ago now barely move the needle.

But I do think something like orchestration remains important, for a few reasons.

First, the world isn't one context window. Real tasks involve many tools, systems, permissions, and people, and parallelism genuinely helps. Even a very capable mind benefits from splitting work, running things concurrently, and isolating contexts so one messy subtask doesn't pollute everything else. That's less about the model being weak and more about the shape of the work.

Second, reliability and accountability. When you deploy agents in places where mistakes are costly, you want checkpoints, verification, and clear boundaries on what each component can touch. That structure is really about trust and governance, and it doesn't disappear when the model gets smarter. If anything it matters more, because the model is being given more autonomy.

Third, cost and latency. You don't want your most expensive model doing every trivial step. Routing simple work to smaller models and reserving the strong one for hard reasoning is just good engineering, and that's a form of orchestration.

So my view is that the orchestration shifts. It moves from humans hand-wiring cognitive steps to the model itself deciding how to decompose a problem, when to spawn helpers, and when to check its work, while humans design the environment: the tools, the permissions, the evaluation signals. The valuable part isn't the intricacy for its own sake. It's having good structure around a capable model, and increasingly the model should be the one building that structure.

r001.rationale: The candidate says orchestration scaffolding compensates for model limits such as weak planning, state management, and error detection.

r002.rationale: It says cost and latency remain reasons for orchestration, giving model routing as an example: smaller models handle simple work while stronger models handle harder reasoning.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not identify achieving the same capability with fewer active parameters as a form of model progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure it will — at least not in the form people imagine today. Let me explain what I mean.

A lot of the orchestration we build right now is compensation. We chain prompts, we add planners, we add reflection loops, we add verifiers, because the base model can't hold a long task in its head, or it drifts, or it hallucinates a tool call. Every one of those layers is a patch over a weakness in the model. And historically, when the model gets stronger, those patches get absorbed. Think about chain-of-thought — that used to be a prompting trick, and now it's basically native behavior. The scaffolding migrated into the weights.

So I'd be cautious about anyone who says the elaborate graph of agents is permanent. Most of it is scaffolding, and scaffolding comes down when the building can stand on its own.

That said, I think there are two things that genuinely survive.

The first is the interface with the real world. No matter how capable the model is, it still has to touch systems that have permissions, latency, failure modes, cost. Someone has to decide what the model is allowed to do, what it needs to confirm before doing, where humans sit in the loop. That's not intelligence, that's governance, and it doesn't go away just because the model got smarter. If anything, a more capable model makes that layer more important, not less, because the actions it can take get more consequential.

The second is decomposition for reasons that aren't about the model's limits. Sometimes you split work across agents because the tasks are genuinely parallel, or because different parts need different data, or different privacy boundaries, or because you want one part to be cheap and fast and another part to be slow and careful. That's engineering, same as any distributed system. A stronger model doesn't change the fact that some problems are naturally structured that way.

So my honest view is: the intricate orchestration — the twenty-node agent graph with handoffs everywhere — I expect that to collapse. The model will just do it. What stays is thinner, more boring, and more about control than cleverness. And I think that's fine. The goal was never to build beautiful orchestration. The goal was to get the task done.

r001.rationale: The response describes orchestration layers as compensation for base-model weaknesses such as losing track of long tasks, drifting, and hallucinating tool calls.

r002.rationale: It says cost can motivate splitting work between cheap, fast agents and slower, careful ones, but it expects intricate orchestration to collapse rather than arguing that cost preserves its value.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe progress as achieving the same capability with fewer active parameters.

astra-6.text:
I think we should separate two things: orchestration that compensates for a model’s weaknesses, and orchestration that reflects the structure of the work. As models improve, a lot of the first kind should disappear. You shouldn’t need five agents just to get one reliable answer.

But complex work still has dependencies, parallel tasks, different information sources, and points where you need verification or human judgment. A stronger model doesn’t make those constraints disappear. It may become much better at deciding how to coordinate them.

So I wouldn’t say intricate orchestration is inherently valuable. The value is in coordinating work effectively. Over time, I’d expect less hand-designed choreography and more coordination that the model creates dynamically—choosing when to delegate, when to check a result, and when the simplest approach is enough.

r001.rationale: The response says orchestration can compensate for model weaknesses and gives using multiple agents to get one reliable answer as an example.

r002.rationale: The response discusses work dependencies, verification, and human judgment, but does not mention cost as a reason orchestration may remain valuable.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss achieving the same capability with fewer active parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think stronger models will change orchestration, but they won’t eliminate the need for it. A model can become much better at an individual task, while the overall system still needs to decide what to work on, what information to share, which tasks can run in parallel, and how to verify the results.

Think about a difficult engineering project. Even if every engineer is very capable, you still benefit from dividing responsibilities and having independent review. With agents, there’s also a practical tradeoff: you don’t necessarily want the most expensive model handling every step. You want to allocate capability where it matters.

But I would distinguish useful orchestration from unnecessary complexity. Some elaborate workflows today compensate for model weaknesses, and those should disappear as models improve. What remains valuable is coordination that reflects the structure of the problem—dependencies, limited resources, independent checks. The orchestration may become more adaptive and less manually specified, but those underlying needs will still exist.

r001.rationale: The response says some elaborate workflows compensate for model weaknesses.

r002.rationale: It says cost remains a practical tradeoff: the most expensive model need not handle every step, so capability should be allocated where it matters.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify achieving the same capability with fewer active parameters as model progress.
